title: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any
goal: By the end you can add an upper bound, a `where` clause or `T : Any` to a type parameter, say what each one lets your code do and which callers it shuts out, and read the matching Java `extends` and `&` syntax.

warmup.q: Which of these compiles: `fun <T> f(x: T) = x.length`, `fun <T> g(x: T) = x.hashCode()`, or `fun <T> h(x: T) { }` called as `h(null)`?
options: Only `f`, because the caller will pass strings
None of them: an unbounded T can do nothing
warmup.why: With no bound, `T` can be any type, nullable ones included, so you may only use what `Any?` has: `hashCode`, `toString`, `==`. `length` is not on every type. And `h(null)` compiles because `T` may be a nullable type. A bound is how you ask for more.

sections.h: An unbounded T can do only what Any? can do
sections.body:
A type parameter with no bound means "some type, I don't know which". So inside the function, `T` can do only what every type can do. In Java the default bound is `Object`. In Kotlin, "every type" includes the nullable ones, so the default bound is **`Any?`**.

```java
static <T> String describe(T x) {
    return "value=" + x + ", hash=" + Objects.hashCode(x);
}

describe("EUR");    // fine
describe(978);      // fine
describe(null);     // fine: any Java T accepts null
```

```kotlin
fun <T> describe(x: T): String = "value=$x, hash=${x.hashCode()}"

describe("EUR")     // fine
describe(978)       // fine
describe(null)      // also fine: T is inferred as Nothing?
```

`toString()`, `hashCode()` and `==` work, because they exist on `Any?`. Anything more specific fails, even when every caller you have in mind would pass a `String`:

```java
static <T> int lengthOf(T x) { return x.length(); }
// error: cannot find symbol: method length()
```

```kotlin
fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length
// error: unresolved reference 'length'.
```

The compiler is not being fussy. Someone could call `lengthOf(42)`, and an `Int` has no `length`. A generic function must work for every type the caller is allowed to pick, so you can use only what all of them share.

Comparison fails the same way. Java says `cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T)`. Kotlin gives a stranger message:

```java
static <T> T bigger(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; }
// error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T)
```

```kotlin
fun <T> bigger(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b
// error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(other: String, ignoreCase: Boolean = ...): Int'
//        is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch.
```

In Kotlin `a > b` means `a.compareTo(b)`. The compiler looks for any `compareTo` it could use on a `T`, finds only the one on `String`, and tells you that one doesn't fit. When an error mentions some unrelated type's method, read it as "this operation is not defined for `T`".

The null case surprises people coming from Java, where every `T` accepts `null` anyway and nobody thinks about it. In Kotlin, `fun <T> f(x: T)` accepts `null` too, because `T` can be `String?` or `Nothing?`. Even an extension like `fun <T> T.describe()` can be called on `null`. If your function must not see null, you have to say so with a bound. Section 4 shows how.

So the job of a bound is to promise more about `T`. The caller can pick fewer types, and in return your code can do more with the one they pick.

try.expect: `describe(null)` prints `value=null, hash=0`: null is a legal `T`. `lengthOf` fails with `Unresolved reference 'length'.` `bigger` fails with a message about `String.compareTo` being inapplicable, because the only `compareTo` the compiler could find is String's. Neither error is about your callers. Both say `T` promises nothing beyond `Any?`. The Java twin fails both with `cannot find symbol`: Java's `T` promises nothing beyond `Object`.

try.title: Make a null mean one thing
steps: Run `NullBoundDemo` (or `NullBoundDemoJava`). Look at the two lines it prints for `pay_1` and `pay_9`.

Change the Kotlin class header to `class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>` and run again. Java has no such bound: in the Java twin, uncomment the `requireNonNull` line instead and see that it fails only when it runs.
Fix `main` so it compiles. How would you now record "checked, no error"? (One answer: store an empty string, or better, a small `sealed interface CheckResult`.)

code.title: NullBoundDemo.kt

alt.title: NullBoundDemoJava.java

try.expect: The first run prints `pay_1 -> null` and `pay_9 -> null`: a stored null and a missing entry look the same. With the bound, `Cache<String, String?>()` no longer compiles: `Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'.` From then on, `get` returning null can only mean "not there".

analogy: A bound is like the requirements line on a job posting. "Any person" (no bound) gets you many applicants, but you can't ask any of them to drive the van. "Must hold a driving licence" (an upper bound) shuts some people out, and in exchange you can hand the keys to whoever turns up. Two requirements (a `where` clause) shrink the pool to people who have both. The analogy breaks in one place: a real employer can interview the candidate and check. The compiler can only trust what the types declare. A class that happens to have a `length` method but does not implement `CharSequence` does not count.
in_your_world: Bounds show up wherever your services compare or key things. A settlement cut-off window over `LocalDate` or `Instant` is a `Window<T : Comparable<T>>`. A generic retry policy that sorts attempts by time needs a comparable timestamp. An in-memory cache in front of the card issuer API, or a store of idempotency responses, should be `Cache<K : Any, V : Any>`, so a `null` from `get` always means "miss" and never "we cached a null". When you call a Java library from Kotlin, its `<T>` allows null, so a Kotlin wrapper with `T : Any` is the place to pin that down.
mistake: The common mistake is leaving a type parameter unbounded and then returning `T?` to mean "absent", as in `fun get(key: K): V?`. It works in every test, because nobody stores a null. Then a caller writes `Cache<String, Instant?>` to remember "we checked and found nothing", and `get` can no longer tell "missing" from "stored null". People make this mistake because the default bound is invisible. The fix is to write `V : Any` whenever `null` has a job in your API, and to model "checked, nothing found" as a real value, not as a stored `null`.

compare.title: Bounds in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Bounds.java

kotlin.title: Bounds.kt

compare.note: The bounds mean the same thing in both languages and compile to the same JVM bounds. Kotlin uses a colon and a `where` clause and does not care about order; Java uses `extends` and `&` and wants the class first. The real difference is nullability. Kotlin's default bound is `Any?`, so you can opt out of null with `T : Any`. Java has no nullable types, so every Java `T` allows null and only annotations can say otherwise. One small surprise: javap shows Kotlin's `T : Comparable<T>` as `<T extends Comparable<? super T>>`, because Kotlin's `Comparable` is declared `in T`. Lesson 5 of this track explains that `? super`.

worked.title: Build a settlement window that works for any comparable type

steps.say: Settlement runs between a cut-off start and end. You want one class for amounts, dates and times. Start without a bound and see what breaks.
1. Ask for exactly the ability you use. The body only compares, so the bound is `T : Comparable<T>`. Now `<=` resolves to `compareTo`.

2. Use it with types that already fit the bound. `LocalDate` and `Instant` are comparable out of the box, so are `Int` and `String`. Self-check: why does `Window(1, "z")` fail? (Both values must be the same `T`, and there is no single `T` that is a `Comparable<T>` for both.)
steps.code:
val cutoff = Window(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6))
LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4) in cutoff        // true

val limits = Window(1_000L, 50_000L)
75_000L in limits                          // false

steps.say: 3. Make your own type fit. A `Money` value with an explicit order is a better fit than raw `Long` cents, and the window needs no change at all.

lab.title: Bound your type parameters: maxOfAll, Window, shortestLabel, coalesce
steps: Run the tests once. All nine fail.
In `Bounds.kt`, write `maxOfAll` with a loop and `>`. Then try deleting `: Comparable<T>` from its signature to see the error, and put it back.
In `Window.kt`, add the `require` in `init`, then write `contains`, `clamp` and `overlaps` using only `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`.
Write `shortestLabel`. It uses `.length` from one bound and `<` from the other.
Write `coalesce`. Notice that the test assigns its result to a plain `String`.
Run the tests until all nine pass.
hints: `require(condition) { "message" }` throws `IllegalArgumentException` when the condition is false.
Two windows do NOT overlap when one ends before the other starts: `endInclusive < other.start || other.endInclusive < start`. Negate that.
In `coalesce`, `if (value != null) return value` smart-casts `value` from `T?` to `T`.

drill.title: Write three bounded signatures from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write only the signatures (no bodies): (1) a function `largest` that returns the biggest item of a `List<T>` for any comparable `T`; (2) a function `trimAndSort` that takes a `List<T>` where `T` is both a `CharSequence` and comparable to itself; (3) a class `Registry` with a key type and a value type, neither of which may be nullable. Then write (1) and (2) in Java.

alt.title: Signatures.java

recap: An unbounded `T` has the bound `Any?`: you can use `toString`, `hashCode` and `==`, and callers may pass `null`.
`T : Comparable<T>` lets you compare two `T` values with `<` and `>`, and rejects types with no natural order at the call site.
More than one bound goes in a `where` clause. At most one bound can be a class. Java writes `<T extends A & B>` with the class first.
`T : Any` rules out nullable type arguments, so `T?` in your API can only mean "absent".
Java type parameters always allow null; Kotlin lets you choose with the bound.

quiz.q: `fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T`. Which call does NOT compile?
options: `maxOf2(Payment("a", 5), Payment("b", 9))` where `Payment` is a plain data class
quiz.why: `Int`, `String` and `LocalDate` are all comparable. A plain data class is not, so the compiler reports `actual type is 'Payment', but 'Comparable<uninferred T ...>' was expected`. Data classes get `equals` and `hashCode`, not an order.

quiz.q: Which signature lets a function call both `x.length` and `x < y` on two `T` values?
options: `fun <T : CharSequence, Comparable<T>> f(x: T, y: T)`
`fun <T> f(x: T, y: T) where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>`
`fun <T : CharSequence & Comparable<T>> f(x: T, y: T)`
quiz.why: Kotlin allows one bound inside the angle brackets. A second bound for the same `T` goes into a `where` clause. The first option declares a second type parameter called `Comparable`, which is not what you meant, and `&` is Java's spelling, not Kotlin's.

quiz.q: A teammate writes `class Cache<K, V> { fun get(key: K): V? }`. Another teammate creates `Cache<String, Instant?>`. What problem appears?
options: It does not compile: `V?` is not allowed when `V` is nullable
`get` returns `null` both for a missing key and for a stored null, so callers can't tell them apart
quiz.why: With the default bound `Any?`, `V` may itself be nullable, and `V?` adds nothing. Declaring `class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>` makes `Cache<String, Instant?>` a compile error, so `null` from `get` always means "missing".

options: `<T extends Number, Comparable<T>>` with the same meaning
quiz.why: In Java the class bound must come first and the interfaces follow after `&`. Putting `Number` second gives `interface expected here`. The comma form declares a second type parameter, and the colon is Kotlin syntax.

quiz.q: From "Generics from zero": what does `val probe: Int = mapOf("EUR" to 100, "USD" to 250L)` make the compiler print?
quiz.why: The assignment to a wrong type is the trick for printing an inferred type. Here the compiler makes the literal `100` a `Long` so that both values share one type. With two values that really differ, such as `1` and `2.5`, you would get an intersection type instead.

flashcards.front: What is the default upper bound of a Kotlin type parameter?
flashcards.back: `Any?`. So an unbounded `T` accepts nullable types, and `fun <T> f(x: T)` can be called with `null`.

flashcards.front: `fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length` gives what error?
flashcards.back: `unresolved reference 'length'.` An unbounded `T` only has the members of `Any?`.

flashcards.front: How do you say "T can be compared with another T"?
flashcards.back: `<T : Comparable<T>>` in Kotlin, `<T extends Comparable<T>>` in Java.

flashcards.front: How do you give one type parameter two bounds in Kotlin?
flashcards.back: A `where` clause: `fun <T> f(x: T) where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>`.

flashcards.front: Why does `where T : Number, T : Exception` fail?
flashcards.back: `only one of the upper bounds can be a class.` A JVM type has one superclass; the other bounds must be interfaces.

flashcards.front: What does `class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>` buy you?
flashcards.back: Neither type argument can be nullable, so `get(): V?` returning null always means "no entry".

flashcards.front: In Java's `<T extends A & B>`, which must come first?
flashcards.back: The class, if there is one. Interfaces follow after `&`. Otherwise javac says `interface expected here`.

terms.plain: A limit on a type parameter: "T must be this type or a subtype of it", written `T : Comparable<T>`.
`Any?`, the bound a Kotlin type parameter has when you write none.
The place for extra bounds on a type parameter: `where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>`.
A bound that mentions the parameter itself, like `T : Comparable<T>`: T can be compared with another T.
A bound that rules out nullable type arguments.
Java's `<T extends A & B>`; the class, if any, must come first.

explain_back.prompt: In your own words: what does adding a bound to a type parameter take away from callers, and what does it give the function body? Use `T : Comparable<T>` and `T : Any` as your two examples.
explain_back.answer: A bound narrows the set of types a caller may pick. In exchange, the function body can rely on more. With no bound, `T` might be anything, including a nullable type, so the body can only use what `Any?` has. With `T : Comparable<T>`, callers can no longer pass types that have no order, like a plain data class, but the body can now use `<` and `>`. With `T : Any`, callers can no longer pick a nullable type, but the body and the API get a guarantee: a `T` is never null, so a `T?` return can only mean "absent". In both cases the compiler enforces the deal at every call site.

deeper.body:
Why does javap show Kotlin's `fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T)` as `<T extends Comparable<? super T>> T maxOf2(T, T)`? Because Kotlin declares `Comparable<in T>`, and when Kotlin writes a Java signature for a parameter of an `in` type, it adds `? super`. That is also why Kotlin accepts `LocalDate`, which is a `Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>` and not a `Comparable<LocalDate>`.

Java's own `Collections.max` shows how messy this gets without declaration-site variance:

```java
public static <T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> coll)
```

```kotlin
fun <T : Comparable<T>> Iterable<T>.max(): T
```

The `Object &` part is there for backward compatibility: it keeps the erased signature returning `Object`, as it did before Java 5. The `? super T` lets a `List<LocalDate>` through. The `? extends T` lets a collection of a subtype through. Kotlin's version gets the same flexibility from `in` and `out` declared once on `Comparable` and `Iterable`. Lessons 4 to 6 of this track build up to reading that Java signature with ease.

One more bound rule: a type parameter bounded by another type parameter can't have extra bounds. `fun <T, U> f(u: U) where U : T, U : Comparable<U>` gives `type parameter cannot have any other bounds if it's bounded by another type parameter.`
